title: FingerTip 20K: A Benchmark for Proactive and Personalized Mobile LLM Agents

response.summary: The paper introduces a potentially valuable benchmark of 21,437 longitudinal, real-device Android interaction episodes from 95 users, targeting proactive intent suggestion and personalized execution. The setting and data are novel and the baseline coverage is useful, but unclear split construction, weakly validated personalization metrics, limited statistical reporting, and substantial privacy/release concerns currently weaken the benchmark’s reliability.
strengths: The benchmark addresses underexplored, practically important capabilities—proactive suggestion and user-specific execution—rather than only instruction-conditioned task completion (pp. 2–5).

The collection is unusually longitudinal and naturalistic, covering 21,437 multi-step episodes and 506 apps on participants’ own devices, with screenshots, accessibility trees, actions, profiles, time, and scenario metadata (pp. 5–6, 14–16).
The paper evaluates a broad set of generalist and GUI-specific agents and includes fine-tuning, input/context ablations, limited out-of-domain tests, and a human comparison (pp. 7–10, 16–19).
weaknesses: The data splits are insufficiently specified and appear numerically inconsistent: the training set has 16,000 episodes, yet is described as sampled from the first 60% of only 21,437 episodes; overlap and leakage among validation and partially overlapping test sets are not fully resolved (p. 16).

The central personalization evidence is weak. Sim2 is a ratio of action-string Levenshtein similarities against one retrieved different-type trace, making it sensitive to coordinates, path length, UI/device differences, and retrieval quality. Its validation uses only four aggregate model points without instance-level correlations, uncertainty, or significance tests (pp. 7–10, 18–19). Likewise, the initial age-based analysis samples only one episode per intent category and reports no controls or statistical tests (pp. 6–7).

Privacy safeguards seem inadequate for public release of longitudinal screenshots and detailed profiles: participants were largely responsible for avoiding private data, automated screening examined only the first and last screenshots, and the paper acknowledges re-identification risk without describing robust redaction or a controlled-access release (pp. 14–15).
response.score_rationale: The naturalistic longitudinal dataset and two user-oriented tracks are meaningful contributions. However, the apparent split inconsistency, confounded personalization metric, limited statistical validation, and unresolved privacy risks prevent the current evidence from firmly supporting a dependable public benchmark. I am somewhat uncertain because the supplied text cannot establish whether the released implementation clarifies the splits or applies additional privacy processing.

response.summary: FingerTip 20K introduces a longitudinal Android dataset from 95 users and two useful tasks: proactive intent suggestion and personalized execution. The resource is potentially valuable, but the proposed personalization evaluation and several empirical/generalization claims are not yet sufficiently rigorous.
strengths: The benchmark targets an important, comparatively underexplored setting and collects 21,437 real-device episodes across 506 apps with temporal, contextual, and user information (pp. 2, 5–6).
Evaluation spans multiple generalist and GUI-specialized agents, with ablations over screenshots, history, and context plus fine-tuning baselines (pp. 8–10, 17–19).
The paper explicitly discusses geographic bias, privacy risks, and the distinction between its two tracks (pp. 14, 17).
weaknesses: Personalization is weakly operationalized: Sim2 is a ratio of Levenshtein similarities between serialized action traces, with an unclear different-user comparator and no control for app/UI/task differences; validation uses only four aggregate model points and lacks correlation statistics or uncertainty (pp. 7–8, 18–19).

The proactive task is inherently underdetermined but is evaluated against one realized intent using text similarity and an LLM binary judge; judge reliability, annotation agreement, variance, and statistical significance are not reported, including for the 400-example human study (p. 8).

Generalization and reproducibility remain limited: main splits retain the same users, unseen tests are very small (three users, seven apps, or four categories), execution uses only 200 dynamic physical-phone episodes with manual success checks, and public fine-grained traces retain acknowledged re-identification risk (pp. 14, 16).
response.score_rationale: The longitudinal collection and task framing are novel enough to be meaningful, and the experiments establish useful baselines. However, the central personalization metric is not convincingly validated, uncertainty and evaluator reliability are largely absent, and the limited execution/generalization setup weakens the headline conclusions. I therefore place the work marginally below acceptance, while noting that stronger metric validation and evaluation protocols could substantially improve it.

response.summary: FingerTip 20K introduces a timely longitudinal dataset and two useful directions for user-oriented mobile agents, backed by broad baseline and ablation experiments. However, the central evaluations do not yet cleanly measure either useful proactivity or genuine personalization, and the real-device protocol and sensitive data release raise reproducibility and privacy concerns.
strengths: The benchmark targets relatively underexplored proactive suggestion and personalized execution settings, with 21,437 longitudinal episodes from 95 users across 506 apps rather than isolated scripted tasks (pp. 2–6).
The empirical study covers general-purpose and GUI-specialized models, fine-tuning, difficulty analyses, contextual ablations, unseen-user/app/intent subsets, and human comparisons (pp. 7–10, 16–19).
The manuscript documents the action space, data format, splits, prompts, demographics, and acknowledged geographic limitations in considerable detail (pp. 6–8, 14–16, 20–21).
weaknesses: The proactive track treats one realized next intent as the sole target and emphasizes exact/similarity matching, without evaluating suggestion usefulness, calibration, abstention, or the cost of intrusive false positives. Human evaluation details and agreement are also absent; even humans reach only 30.3% under this formulation (pp. 8, 17–18).

The personalization construct is weakly validated. Levenshtein similarity over action strings can primarily reflect app layout, coordinates, device state, and task path rather than preference; its denominator uses a nearest task from a different coarse age group. Figure 5 lacks controlled task/app/device matching, uncertainty, or significance tests, while the claimed human validation uses only four aggregate model points (pp. 7–8, 18–19). Same-user temporal splits further allow fine-tuning gains to reflect memorized routines rather than transferable personalization (pp. 10, 16).

Execution evaluation is only 200 episodes on dynamic physical-phone apps, uses manual success judgments without reported annotator agreement, and is difficult to reproduce as app states evolve (pp. 7–9, 16). Releasing longitudinal screenshots, accessibility trees, timestamps, profiles, and actions also presents substantial re-identification risk that the paper itself acknowledges; the described filtering and consent process does not establish strong privacy guarantees (pp. 14–16).
response.score_rationale: The dataset and problem framing are valuable and plausibly novel, but validity concerns affect both headline tracks, especially the claim that Sim2 measures personalization. Limited reproducibility and material privacy risks keep the work marginally below acceptance despite its scale and extensive experiments. Some uncertainty remains because dataset quality and release safeguards cannot be independently inspected from the manuscript alone.

response.summary: FingerTip 20K introduces a timely benchmark built from 21,437 longitudinal, real-device interaction episodes from 95 users, targeting proactive intent suggestion and personalized execution. The resource is potentially valuable, but the central evaluation—especially the operationalization of personalization—has substantial validity and statistical-reporting weaknesses, leaving the main claims only partially supported.
strengths: The benchmark targets proactive suggestion and user-specific execution, two useful settings largely absent from the compared mobile-agent benchmarks, and supplies longitudinal context rather than isolated tasks (pp. 2–5).
The collection is unusually broad in episodes and applications and includes screenshots, accessibility trees, actions, intents, profiles, time, and location from real devices (pp. 5–6, 15–16).
The paper evaluates diverse baselines and includes contextual ablations, limited out-of-domain tests, fine-tuning studies, and a human comparison (pp. 8–10, 16–19).
weaknesses: The personalization construct is not convincingly isolated: Sim2 compares string-level action similarity against one trace from a differently age-binned user, making it sensitive to task, app/UI state, coordinates, device, and trace length rather than uniquely to preference. The validation reports only four model-level averages without correlations, uncertainty, or controls (pp. 7–8, 18–19).

Evaluation reliability is underreported: proactive success relies on an unvalidated DeepSeek-V3 judge; execution uses only 200 manually judged dynamic-app episodes; and tables provide no repeated runs, confidence intervals, inter-rater agreement, or significance tests (pp. 8, 16). Thus several reported improvements may not be robust.

The same-user temporal split permits memorization of recurring intents and traces, while unseen-user/app/intent subsets are very small and the personalized-history construction is insufficiently specified (pp. 16–17). Releasing longitudinal screenshots, accessibility trees, profiles including address, timestamps, and user IDs also presents serious re-identification risk beyond the paper's manual/VLM filtering (pp. 14–16).
response.score_rationale: The real-world longitudinal dataset and new task framing are notable, but the benchmark's key personalization metric and evaluation protocol have central construct-validity and uncertainty problems. I therefore place it marginally below acceptance pending stronger metric validation, statistically rigorous evaluation, clearer split/history controls, and a safer release plan.

response.summary: FingerTip 20K introduces a substantial longitudinal mobile-interaction dataset and two timely tracks: proactive intent suggestion and preference-aware execution. The collection and baseline suite are valuable, but the benchmark’s central personalization metric and evaluation design do not yet convincingly isolate user preference from task/UI similarity, and privacy and statistical-validity details are insufficient.
strengths: The dataset is unusually large and longitudinal for mobile GUI research: 21,437 episodes from 95 users across 506 apps, with screenshots, accessibility trees, actions, profiles, time, and location (pp. 2, 5–6, 15–16).

The two proposed tracks address important, underexplored capabilities beyond instruction-following, and the paper evaluates diverse generalist and GUI-specialized baselines plus fine-tuning (pp. 4–5, 7–10).
Useful supplementary analyses examine contextual-input ablations, unseen users/apps/intents, cross-track transfer, and human ratings of personalization (pp. 16–19).
weaknesses: Sim2 is not a well-validated personalization measure: it compares string-level action sequences against one retrieved trace from an age-based “different type” user, so coordinates, app/UI state, task mismatch, path length, and device differences can dominate genuine preference. The validation uses only four aggregate model-level points, without correlations, uncertainty, or per-example analysis (pp. 7–8, 18–19).

The evidence lacks statistical rigor and key evaluation detail: no confidence intervals or repeated runs are reported; proactive success relies partly on an LLM judge; execution success is manually judged without annotator counts/agreement; and conclusions rely on only 200 execution episodes. The unseen-user analysis contains just three users and does not clearly specify what history remains available (pp. 8, 16).

Privacy safeguards appear inadequate for publicly releasing intimate longitudinal screenshots and accessibility trees: participants were asked to avoid private data, and automated screening examined only the first and last screenshots before human rechecking. No ethics-board review is stated, despite acknowledged re-identification risk (pp. 14–15).
response.score_rationale: The benchmark direction and data collection are potentially impactful, and fine-tuning gains suggest utility. However, because the principal personalization claim rests on a confounded metric and the small-scale evaluations lack uncertainty and annotation-reliability reporting, the current evidence is marginally below the standard needed to establish a reliable benchmark.
